"executive_summary": "Proteins are normally built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional chemistry can enhance stability. Researchers have created artificial topological proteins such as cyclic, lasso, and catenane proteins, but these usually contain multiple domains, which complicates the study of topological effects. The authors hypothesized that a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of chemical topology and provide an unusual scaffold for engineering. They report cat-DHFR, a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase, made by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement. The synthesis was accomplished in cells using programmed post-translational processing without additional in vitro reactions. The target molecule, P-2, contains few exogenous motifs and was characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability and shows enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The results suggest that linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents an entirely new horizon in protein science. The design used the original fold itself as the entangling template, eliminating the need for an exogenous entangling motif. Cleavage between residues 88 and 89 generated two highly intertwined segments with a Gaussian linking number of +0.726, which upon cyclization gave a cat-DHFR with a GLN of +1.120. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24, and rewired loops of at least 16 residues bridged the split motifs. The streamlined biosynthesis used two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs. Protein expression was carried out at 16 o C for 20 h in E.coli BL21(DE3) competent cells, and proteins were purified using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion chromatography. SDS-PAGE showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The identities were confirmed by accurate molecular weights in LC-MS spectra. The far-UV CD spectra showed that cat-DHFR remains folded but has reduced intensities of both positive and negative peaks, suggesting a loosening of the secondary structure. The near-UV CD spectrum exhibited a positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to the linear control. The catalytic activity of cat-DHFR was lower (~5 U/mg) than the linear control (~14 U/mg), but it remarkably retains a significant portion of the activity. The Km of cat-DHFR was approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR, and the kcat was about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency was reduced by an order of magnitude. The disassociation constants were generally much larger for cat-DHFR than for l-DHFR, with ~173-fold for DHF and ~14-fold for NADPH. The KD between cat-DHFR and the product, THF, was increased by ~3.6-fold relative to l-DHFR. The reduced enzymatic activity should be mainly attributed to the compromised affinity of cat-DHFR towards substrate and cofactor. cat-DHFR also preserved more activity (87%) than l-DHFR (74%) in the presence of 5% DMSO. Both results suggest that mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience of the enzyme. The authors envision that the reduced activity may be further restored to match, if not surpass, that of the linear control by directed evolution. This work demonstrates the feasibility of converting a model enzyme into its single-domain catenane counterpart, which could lead to enhanced protein stability and provide an unusual scaffold for further engineering and evolution.",

summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang, Tianzuo Li, Jiyeon Lee, Dahye Lim, Lianjie Xu, Yajie Liu, Jongcheol Seo, Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.type_of_paper: Research article (design and synthesis of a novel protein topology)
summary.executive_summary: Proteins are normally built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity, yet natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional chemistry can enhance stability. Researchers have created artificial topological proteins such as cyclic, lasso, and catenane proteins, but these usually contain multiple domains, which complicates the study of topological effects. The authors hypothesized that a single-domain topological protein would show the most profound impact of chemical topology and provide an unusual scaffold for engineering. They report cat-DHFR, a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase, made by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement. The synthesis was accomplished in cells using programmed post-translational processing without additional in vitro reactions. The target molecule, P-2, contains few exogenous motifs and was characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability and shows enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. The results suggest that linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents an entirely new horizon in protein science. The design used the original fold itself as the entangling template, eliminating the need for an exogenous entangling motif. Cleavage between residues 88 and 89 generated two highly intertwined segments with a Gaussian linking number of +0.726, which upon cyclization gave a cat-DHFR with a GLN of +1.120. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24, and rewired loops of at least 16 residues bridged the split motifs. The streamlined biosynthesis used two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs. Protein expression was carried out at 16 o C for 20 h in E.coli BL21(DE3) competent cells, and proteins were purified using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion chromatography. SDS-PAGE showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The identities were confirmed by accurate molecular weights in LC-MS spectra. The far-UV CD spectra showed that cat-DHFR remains folded but has reduced intensities of both positive and negative peaks, suggesting a loosening of the secondary structure. The near-UV CD spectrum exhibited a positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to the linear control. The catalytic activity of cat-DHFR was lower (~5 U/mg) than the linear control (~14 U/mg), but it remarkably retains a significant portion of the activity. The Km of cat-DHFR was approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR, and the kcat was about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency was reduced by an order of magnitude. The disassociation constants were generally much larger for cat-DHFR than for l-DHFR, with ~173-fold for DHF and ~14-fold for NADPH. The KD between cat-DHFR and the product, THF, was increased by ~3.6-fold relative to l-DHFR. The reduced enzymatic activity should be mainly attributed to the compromised affinity of cat-DHFR towards substrate and cofactor. cat-DHFR also preserved more activity (87%) than l-DHFR (74%) in the presence of 5% DMSO. Both results suggest that mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience of the enzyme. The authors envision that the reduced activity may be further restored to match, if not surpass, that of the linear control by directed evolution. This work demonstrates the feasibility of converting a model enzyme into its single-domain catenane counterpart, which could lead to enhanced protein stability and provide an unusual scaffold for further engineering and evolution.

Research Context
Proteins are normally built from linear polypeptide chains, which limits their topological diversity. Natural protein domains can exist independently, fold autonomously, and evolve dynamically, making them valuable modules for engineering. Natural topological proteins suggest that unconventional chemistry could enhance protein stability relative to linear counterparts. Topology has been recognized as a unique dimension for protein engineering in recent years. Artificial topological proteins have advanced tremendously through assembly-reaction synergy. Artificial topological proteins include star proteins, cyclic proteins, lasso proteins, protein catenanes, and protein pretzelanes. The approach often involves the use of genetically encoded entangling motifs and reaction motifs. Artificial topological proteins synthesized to date usually contain multiple domains, complicating the study of topological effects. A single-domain topological protein would exhibit the most profound impact of chemical topology. It remains challenging to prepare single-domain topological proteins, even for the simplest catenane or Hopf link. DHFR catalyzes the reduction of DHF to THF in the presence of NADPH.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a single-domain topological protein can be designed and synthesized. The authors hypothesize that single-domain topological proteins would show the most profound impact of chemical topology. They predict that single-domain topological proteins would provide an unusual scaffold for engineering and evolution. The authors envision that the need for an exogenous entangling motif may be eliminated by exploiting spatially entangled relationships. They hypothesize that single-domain protein catenanes may be designed with identical composition to the linear wild-type. The authors predict that linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with well-preserved function. They expect that the reduced activity may be further restored to match, if not surpass, that of the linear control. The authors predict that mechanical interlocking would enhance the thermal resilience of the enzyme.

Methodological Details
The study focused on DHFR from Escherichia coli as a model enzyme. The target molecule, P-2, contains few exogenous motifs. The design was achieved by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement. The synthesis was accomplished by programmed streamlined post-translational processing events in cells. The synthesis was accomplished without any additional in vitro reactions. The target was characterized by combined techniques of LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Cleavage between residues 88 and 89 generated two highly intertwined segments. The split of DHFR that gives the largest GLN was believed to possess the potential entangling core. The design was composed of residues 1-88 as one ring and residues 89-159 as the other ring. The two fragments are known to reconstitute efficiently. The entangling core of the design was similar to that of the wild-type. The cat-DHFR had a GLN of +1.120.

Procedures And Architectures
The streamlined biosynthesis used two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs. The split DHFR itself was used as the entangled template. The length of the new loop and the sites of ring closure should be carefully chosen. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. The rewired loops were designed to be long enough to bridge the split structural motifs. The gene cassette contained two DHFR segments as the entangling template. The gene cassette contained two mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs for ring closure. The gene cassette contained the tobacco etch virus protease recognition sequence in the first ring. The genes were sub-cloned to pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors for expression. The plasmids were used to transform E.coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Protein expression was carried out at 16 o C for 20 h to ensure proper folding. Proteins were purified under native conditions using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography.

Key Results
SDS-PAGE showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR. SDS-PAGE showed a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. There were some faint bands at lower molecular weights, likely attributed to the individual component rings. The apparently faster mobility of cat-DHFR in SDS-PAGE was reasonable because the concatenated form tends to be much more compact. cat-DHFR elutes as a much broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume than l-DHFR. The identities of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR were confirmed by their accurate molecular weights in LC-MS spectra. The far-UV CD spectra showed that cat-DHFR remains folded but has reduced intensities of both positive and negative peaks. The near-UV CD spectrum exhibited a positive ellipticity at ~290 nm similar to the linear control. The catalytic activity of cat-DHFR was lower (~5 U/mg) than the linear control (~14 U/mg). The previously reported rethreaded DHFR shows no reducing activity at all. The reconstituted physical complex of two DHFR fragments retained only 15% of the enzymatic activity. cat-DHFR remarkably retains a significant portion of the activity.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Km of cat-DHFR was approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR. The kcat of cat-DHFR was about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency of cat-DHFR was reduced by an order of magnitude. cat-DHFR has a lower affinity toward substrates, a lower turnover rate, and a decreased catalytic efficiency. The disassociation constants were generally much larger for cat-DHFR than for l-DHFR. The KD was ~173-fold for DHF and ~14-fold for NADPH. The binding of NADPH significantly enhances the affinity of cat-DHFR towards DHF. The KD between cat-DHFR and the product, THF, was increased by ~3.6-fold relative to l-DHFR. The reduced enzymatic activity should be mainly attributed to the compromised affinity of cat-DHFR towards substrate and cofactor. cat-DHFR preserved more activity (87%) than l-DHFR (74%) in the presence of 5% DMSO. Both results suggest that mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience of the enzyme. The results suggest that linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with elevated stability.

The authors have not been able to obtain a crystal structure of cat-DHFR. The failure to crystallize may be due to unsatisfactory purity, disordered linkers, or reduced binding affinity. The authors had to resort to indirect ways of characterization, such as proteolytic digestion experiment. The current approach requires extensive optimization to achieve the assembly-reaction synergy. Much less catenane product was formed with the construct using split-intein ligation pairs on the same side. Considerable amounts of single-ring side products were formed (~33% of catenane form). The steric hindrance of the bulky split-intein pairs affects the correct reconstitution efficiency. The method is generally robust before the linker becomes too short. The yield with the shortest linker is only about one-fifth that of the longest. The reduced activity may be further restored to match, if not surpass, that of the linear control.
